artworks.title: The Glass House
artworks.description: A pavilion for looking at the landscape: 55 by 33 feet, with a glass door in the middle of each wall. Johnson lived here from 1949 until his death in 2005. There are no walls inside, but he called the areas “rooms”: kitchen, dining, living room, bedroom, hearth and a brick cylinder with the bathroom. Most of the furniture is by Mies van der Rohe, who designed the daybed for Johnson. Johnson said it was the only house where you can see the sunset and the moonrise at once.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: The Glass House (1949): Johnson’s home, 55 by 33 feet of glass
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Brick House
artworks.description: The other half of the composition: as long as the Glass House but half as deep, and almost windowless, with round windows at the back (after Brunelleschi’s dome in Florence). It holds the heating and support for both houses. In 1953 Johnson remade the inside: a skylit corridor with prints by Brice Marden, a reading room with his own library, and a bedroom under low white vaults after Sir John Soane, lined in Fortuny fabric. Restored in 2024.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: The Brick House (1949): guest house and bedroom with the Soane-style vault, Johnson’s reading room
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Painting Gallery
artworks.description: Half sunk into a grassy mound with a red sandstone entrance, so it would not spoil the view from the Glass House. Inside are three round rooms with rotating racks like postcard stands: two paintings per spindle, 42 in all, six on show at a time. Works by Frank Stella, Andy Warhol, Robert Rauschenberg, David Salle, Cindy Sherman and Julian Schnabel. You may walk up onto the roof.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Painting Gallery (1965): a grass-covered berm with three round rooms of rotating racks
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Sculpture Gallery
artworks.description: Inspired by Greek island villages where “every street is a staircase”: squares at 45 degrees, stairs spiralling down past bays of sculpture, under a glass roof whose steel rafters cast patterns of light. Johnson called it the best single room he ever designed. Skylights replaced in 2015.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Sculpture Gallery (1970): five levels under a glass roof, Johnson’s “best single room”
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Studio (Library)
artworks.description: Johnson’s one-room library and workplace, “an air-conditioned monk’s cell”, reached through a field of tall grass: 1,400 architecture books, a fireplace, no bathroom, light from the skylight in its cone. From the Glass House dining table he watched the light change on the cone.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: The Studio (1980): Johnson’s library and workroom, with a cone-shaped roof
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Ghost House
artworks.description: A folly of chain-link fence in the shape of a simple house, on the stone foundation of a burnt barn: a nod to Frank Gehry’s ordinary materials and to Venturi and Scott Brown. It kept animals off the lilies inside.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Ghost House (1984): a chain-link “house” on an old barn foundation
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: Da Monsta
artworks.description: Johnson’s last building here, by the entrance: warped, torqued walls of sprayed concrete, far from the straight lines of the International Style. First called “Dresden Zwei” after a museum design by Frank Stella; the name came from a talk with the critic Herbert Muschamp. Today it holds the exhibitions.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Da Monsta (1995): Johnson’s last building on the site, by the entrance
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: Pavilion in the Pond
artworks.description: Prefabricated concrete arches on the edge of the pond Johnson dug, built smaller than life so it looks further away: a tall person can’t stand up inside, and a child “feels like a king”. It once had a 20-foot fountain.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Pavilion in the Pond (1962): a folly built at a smaller scale
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: Monument to Lincoln Kirstein
artworks.description: A 30-foot tower of stacked concrete blocks and steep steps, “a staircase to nowhere”, named for Johnson’s friend who founded the New York City Ballet. Kirstein chose an inscription for the top step, which only climbers read.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Monument to Lincoln Kirstein (1985): a 30-foot climbable tower of concrete blocks
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: Popestead, Calluna Farms and Grainger
artworks.description: Three older houses Johnson and his partner David Whitney bought and restored: Popestead (a barn turned house), Calluna Farms (Whitney’s home, 1905) and Grainger (an 18th-century central-chimney house). Not open on regular tours.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Popestead (c. 1920, a barn turned house): not open on regular tours
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Succulent Garden
artworks.description: David Whitney’s garden in front of Calluna, laid out after a Suprematist drawing by Kazimir Malevich, on pink granite left over from Johnson’s AT&T Building.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: David Whitney’s Succulent Garden (1989), in front of Calluna
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The Peony Garden
artworks.description: Whitney’s garden at Grainger: 10 tree peonies, 41 peonies and 25 irises, with Alessandro Twombly’s sculpture Nature Amassment #4. Only Whitney was allowed to work in it.
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: Grainger (c. 1783), with Whitney’s Peony Garden: not open on regular tours
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: The landscape
artworks.description: Johnson bought the first five acres in 1945 and, with Whitney, grew the site to 49. Old stone walls, barn foundations and big trees became its “organizing principle”; woods were cleared to open views to buildings he called “events on the landscape”, after English gardens such as Stourhead and Stowe. “To me, it’s one art.”
artworks.imageCredit: The Glass House (National Trust for Historic Preservation)
artworks.galleryName: The Glass House grounds: 49 acres of lawns, meadows and woods with 14 structures. Visit on a tour only (outline approximate)
artworks.placeNote: Place from the Glass House’s own site map.

artworks.title: Philip Johnson
artworks.medium: Acrylic and silkscreen inks on canvas
artworks.description: Acrylic and silkscreen inks on canvas · Nine panels, H 32” x W 32”; H 96” x W 96” · Andy Warhol, a successful commercial illustrator in the 1950s, began to paint images derived from the comic strips and advertisements in 1960. By 1962, he was a leading Pop artist who used the silkscreen process to transfer photographic images derived from the mass media and popular culture to canvas. Philip Johnson and David Whitney were among his most important supporters. Johnson donated several major paintings, among them the iconic Gold Marilyn Monroe of 1962, as gifts to the Museum of Modern Art. Johnson frequently commissioned Warhol to create works for buildings he designed, the most famous example being Thirteen Most Wanted Men intended for the New York State Pavilion at the 1964 World’s Fair. Due to Governor Nelson Rockefeller’s objections to its content, Warhol had it covered with silver paint. David Whitney organized the exhibition Andy Warhol: Portraits of the 70s, in 1979 for the Whitney Museum of American Art. · The single major Warhol remaining in the Painting Gallery is a portrait of Philip Johnson from 1972. This painting, which repeats the same pensive image of the architect nine times in a grid format, is rendered in a subdued, earth-tone palette. · • Exhibited in inaugural exhibition Johns, Stella, Warhol: Works in Series, organized by David Whitney at the Art Museum of South Texas, Texas A&M University, Corpus Christi in 1972 · • Gift of David Whitney to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, 1998 · • Conserved in-situ by Luca Bonetti, 2009 · • Published in Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, Volume 3: Paintings and Sculptures 1970–1974, edited by Neil Printz and Executive Editor Sally King-Nero, Andy Warhol Foundation by Phaidon Press, 2010. The Painting Gallery’s racks rotate: ask whether it is out today.

artworks.title: Two Circus Women
artworks.medium: Papier mache on plaster armature with internal bamboo braces
artworks.description: Papier mache on plaster armature with internal bamboo braces · H 62” x W 42” x D 18” · A leading modernist sculptor of the first half of the twentieth century, Elie Nadelman pursued a highly individual path. Although this Polish-born artist was among the first to practice abstraction in sculpture in Paris, where he was a prominent member of the avant-garde, he later devoted himself to the human figure. The source of his work ranged from early classicism to Asian and Egyptian sculpture to American folk art. Nadelman relocated to New York in 1914 and became well established in the New York art world, appreciated for his work in bronze, marble, wood, and more. · Whereas Nadelman’s early work tended to present sleek, stylized figures, in the mid-twenties his style shifted. Working with papier mache over plaster armatures, he began to focus on images of female circus performers with bulbous contours and indistinct facial features, as seen in Two Circus Women, 1930. Although this work met with little favor in its own time, it was greatly appreciated by Philip Johnson. Two decades after Nadelman’s death, Johnson used this sculpture as the maquette for a work three times its size carved in white Carrara marble for the atrium of his and John Burgee’s New York State Theater at Lincoln Center. · • Acquired in 1949 from Artist’s Estate · • Used as cast for bronze copy for Nelson A. Rockefeller, 1951 · • Used as pointing model for monumental marble sculpture commissioned for New York State Theatre, 1964 · • Extensively repaired by Joseph Turnbach, 1969 and 1981 · • Conserved by Daria Keynan; project funded in part with a matching grant from the Historic Sites Fund, 2010

artworks.title: Averroes
artworks.description: Aluminum paint on canvas · H 73-3/16” x W 71-5/8” · Over the course of several decades, Philip Johnson amassed one of the most extensive collections of work by Frank Stella. Fourteen major pieces by Stella spanning the years 1960 to 1990 and representing eleven separate series are found on the Glass House property. Philip Johnson was an avid, early collector of Stella and he donated Astoria, 1958, a transitional work that preceded the “Black Painting Series” with which Stella emerged on the New York scene in 1959, to the Museum of Modern Art. · Stella was among the first artists of the twentieth century to spend his entire career working within the realm of abstraction. While he began with striped painting distinctive for their internal logic and reductive natures, Stella then moved, in series after series, into increasingly irregular and elaborate structures and progressively improvisational modes of working. Eventually, his works came to assume fully sculptural dimensions. His freestanding, gleaming metal Raft of the Medusa, Part I, 1990, unfolds dramatically in space; both its title and dynamic form allude to Gericault’s famed painting of 1819. · From Artist’s Aluminum series · From Artist’s first solo exhibition at Leo Castelli Gallery, 1960 · Among the Artist’s first shaped canvases · First artwork acquired from Leo Castelli Gallery by Philip Johnson at the advice of David Whitney in 1961 · Originally mounted on masonite; masonite removed and conserved by Daniel Goldreyer, 1967 · Conserved in-situ by Luca Bonetti, 2007. The Painting Gallery’s racks rotate: ask whether it is out today.

artworks.title: Burial of Phocion
artworks.description: Nicolas Poussin (attributed to) · Burial of Phocion, ca. 1648-49 · Oil on canvas, backed with panel · H 47-3/4” x W 59-3/4” · Overall height with stand, 76” · Nicolas Poussin defined French Baroque classicism in painting. With the exception of two years serving as court painter to Louis XIII, Poussin spent his entire career in Rome, where he specialized in history paintings – scenes from ancient history, mythology, and the Bible – notable for their dramatic clarity and nobility of purpose. Burial of Phocion depicts the funeral of an Athenian general put to death because he refused to conceal the truth. The idealized landscape, with its almost mathematically precise spaces, is a memorial to Stoic virtue. · A permanent fixture of the Glass House’s main pavilion since its construction i 1949, the painting remains one of only two artworks on view in the Glass House (the other being an sculpture by Elie Nadelman). The installation of Burial of Phocion in the Glass House, although suggested by Aldred H. Barr, Jr., the founding Director of the Museum of Modern Art, is revealing of Johnson’s conception of landscape. His childhood on an Ohio farm, with its spatial stability and rational order, is manifested in the Connecticut property in the studied placement of pavilions and buildings and the selective removal of trees. The Poussin serves as a mediator between the interior geometry of the Glass House and the tamed exterior landscape seen through its transparent walls. · • Acquired in 1945 from Julius H. Weitzner Gallery · • Previously conserved by Margaret Watherston, 1957 and 1961; Helen B. Mannoni, 1968-69; and Rustin Levenson, 1981 · • Conserved by Luca Bonetti, 2007-08
